title: Turning one-off jobs into repeat clients
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who want past clients to call again
learningOutcomes: Plan a follow-up sequence for past clients that is accurate, consented and respectful of unsubscribe requests.
Design a check-in or maintenance package with a defined scope, price, exclusions and cancellation terms.
Record repeat work and referrals against each client, so their value can be measured.

instruction.heading: Why repeat work changes the business
instruction.body: Most property trade enquiries are one-off jobs, so a business can end up in a constant search for new clients. Repeat work reduces that pressure. A client who trusts the business will call again for the next small job, and that client is more likely to recommend it to friends and neighbours. The aim is a base of clients who call regularly, while the business still takes new work. Repeat work also makes the week easier to plan, which reduces the admin load described in “Owner time and admin workload before the first job”.

instruction.heading: Staying in touch after the job
instruction.body: Contact the client a few days after the job to check that the work is performing as expected, and ask for a review if the client is pleased. Then plan a light touch two or three times a year, such as a seasonal reminder or an offer to inspect the property. Keep messages short and useful. A message that gives a real reason to reply, such as a seasonal check or a warning about a known issue, works better than one that only says hello. Electronic messages must follow the Spam Act 2003, which requires consent, accurate sender identification and an unsubscribe option that works. The ACMA guidance, checked on 2026-11-02, says unsubscribe requests must be acted on within five working days. The wider outreach rules are set out in “Finding your first customers through direct, consent-based outreach” and “Referrals and repeat work from existing clients”.

instruction.heading: Designing a check-in or maintenance package
instruction.body: A package bundles a defined set of services into a regular arrangement at a set price. For example, a yearly property check with a fixed list of items, a set number of minor repairs and one price. The package must be clearly defined: what is included, what is excluded, what happens when extra work is needed, how often it runs and how the client can cancel. Check the margin of the package against the hourly rate and minimum charge (“Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”), because a package that suits the client but does not cover the time loses money.

instruction.heading: Offering repeat-client terms carefully
instruction.body: Discounts for repeat clients can help, but only when the business can afford them. Calculate any discount as a percentage of the normal price, and check the margin after it is applied. Benefits that cost less than a discount may be better, such as priority booking or a free annual inspection with a defined scope. Record the benefit in writing so the client knows what to expect.

procedure: Record each client's job history, consent and preferred contact method in the client record.
Send a follow-up message a few days after each job, asking for a review if the client is happy.
Plan two or three light-touch contacts a year, each with a useful reason.
Design one package with a defined scope, price, exclusions, frequency and cancellation terms.
Check the package margin against the hourly rate and minimum charge before offering it.
Record each repeat job and referral against the client, and review the totals every quarter.

workedExamples.situation: An owner has twelve past clients and wants to offer an annual check. The check includes a walk-through, a short list of minor fixes and a discount on any extra work.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must the package state before the owner offers it?
workedExamples.reasoning: The package must set out what the walk-through covers, how many minor fixes are included and roughly how long each may take, what is excluded, how extra work is priced and approved, how often the check runs, and how the client cancels. The owner should check, using “Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”, that the package price covers the time and the materials before making the offer. Contact must respect each client's consent and any unsubscribe request.

equipmentAndPpe: Client record with consent and contact preferences
Package terms sheet with inclusions, exclusions and cancellation terms

commonErrors.error: Sending repeat marketing to clients who did not consent, or who asked to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Record consent, and act on each unsubscribe request within five working days.

commonErrors.error: Offering a package without a defined scope, which leads to disputes about extra work.
commonErrors.prevention: State what is included and excluded, and how extra work is priced and approved.

commonErrors.error: Discounting repeat work so far that the job is unprofitable.
commonErrors.prevention: Check every discount and package against the hourly rate and minimum charge.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Electronic messages to clients and past clients must follow the Spam Act 2003, as shown on the ACMA guidance checked on 2026-11-02.
Package terms, cancellation rights and the rules on unfair terms must be checked before a package is published.
A package that includes electrical, gas or plumbing work is limited to what the owner is permitted to do. Other work must be referred, and the package must say so. This lesson grants no licence.

qualityStandard: Every repeat-contact message is linked to a recorded consent and includes an unsubscribe option.
Each package has a defined scope, price, exclusions, frequency and cancellation terms.
Repeat work and referrals are recorded against each client.
documentationEvidence: Client record with job history, consent and contact preferences
Package terms sheet with inclusions, exclusions and cancellation terms
Quarterly review of repeat work and referrals
summary: Keep past clients in touch with useful messages that they have consented to.
A package needs a defined scope, a price and clear cancellation terms.
Check every repeat discount against the margin.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the main risk of a repeat-client package with no defined scope?
options: The client will receive too many reviews each week
Disputes about what is included and how extra work is priced
The Spam Act will apply to the package itself and to every client
The package will need a licence before it can be sold

knowledgeChecks.question: A past client has asked to stop receiving text messages. What must the owner do?
options: Keep texting, because the client is already known and the texts are short and friendly
Remove the client from future messages promptly, and within five working days at the latest
Ask a friend to send the next message and let them choose the wording and the time
Wait for the client to ask again and then send the next promotional text message

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should the margin of a repeat-client discount be checked?
options: So the discount can be doubled
So the job does not become unprofitable
So the client receives a larger invoice
So the owner can avoid recording the discount

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam
officialReferences.covers: ACMA guidance on the Spam Act 2003: consent is required before marketing messages, and keeping a record of express consent is advised; inferred consent is less reliable than express consent; the sender must be identified accurately with correct contact details kept for at least 30 days; every commercial message must contain an unsubscribe option that is clear, free, needs no account or extra personal information, and works for at least 30 days; unsubscribe requests must be honoured within 5 working days. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA). This is a summary of the guidance, not the Act text, which was not read.
